title: "...let's not let this turn into an inferno." 2026
author: Lance Eaton
summary: In part two of an interview conducted by Lance Eaton, higher-education faculty Daryl Privott and Casey Cosgriff of Morehead State University discuss developing a 'LOVE and wisdom' framework for approaching generative AI in teacher-education programs, describing the effort as a way to give overworked institutions 'breathing room' rather than another item added to an already smoldering workload. Casey describes using generative AI itself to analyze how the technology will affect all ten InTASC teacher-preparation standards, while Daryl frames the framework's real purpose as giving faculty language to tell administrators that responsible implementation takes time, invoking Gagne's nine events of instruction as a baseline literacy anyone making education policy should possess. The conversation names a specific obstacle to institutional adoption, territorialism, illustrated by their LOVE-framework grant proposal receiving lukewarm reception, and situates the framework within Morehead State's specific identity as an Appalachian teachers college. Casey's closing anecdote about his own teenage son's survey, finding roughly a third of his high school peers had used AI to cheat in the past week, is used to argue both teachers and learners must change because AI cheating on 'mindless assignments' cannot be addressed by simply continuing the same worksheet-based practices. Throughout, the interviewees stress that their book chapter itself was co-developed using generative AI, treating that iterative co-authorship as evidence of the framework's practical applicability rather than a contradiction.
points: Names 'invisible labor' as the specific mechanism by which corporate 'do more with less' logics harm nonprofit educational institutions, arguing the burden of recognizing and naming this dynamic falls on those who already see it happening.

Uses the oil-fire-versus-paper-fire metaphor to argue institutional crises require diagnosis before response, since treating every problem-fire the same way (dousing with the same generic solution) fails when the underlying cause differs.

Cites Gagne's nine events of instruction as a concrete, testable baseline literacy standard, arguing anyone making policy that affects educators and students should be expected to know it before doing so.

Reports a specific institutional obstacle (territorialism) that caused a federal FIPSE grant proposal built on their LOVE framework to be poorly received, offering a candid account of adoption friction rather than only success stories.

Grounds the abstract AI-in-education debate in a concrete family data point: a high-school student's own survey finding roughly a third of peers had used AI to cheat in the past week, used to argue worksheet-based assignments themselves need to change, not just detection policy.
quotes: I grapple with higher ed having been on fire, really on fire the last year or so, reasonably on fire the last few years, and smoldering for at least the 20 years I've been in it.
if you don't know Gagne's nine events of instruction, you shouldn't be making policy around education and educators
Generative AI is another thing that gets brought in and adds to the fire, as you said, the smoldering. How do we take a moment and say, let's not let this turn into an inferno?
When corporate logics enter environments where people don't have the language or framework to recognize what's happening, the burden falls on those of us who do see it to call it out.
When things are on fire, yes, you want to put them out, but you have to know what kind of fire it is. An oil fire is different from a paper fire.
Casey and I proposed the LOVE framework as the foundation for the grant. It wasn't necessarily received very well. There's some territorialism.

About a third of those admitted using AI in the last week for some kind of cheating. His takeaway was that schools and teachers can't just keep doing the same thing: you can't hand out worksheets and mindless assignments, because you'll just get mindless use of AI to do them.
